guides.summary: GitHub is the easy case. Anyone with a GitHub account can register an OAuth app in a few minutes, and there is no review or approval step. The main decision is whether you want an OAuth app or a GitHub App: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps for fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens.

composio.note: Composio provides a managed OAuth app for GitHub, so you only need your own app if you want your app name on the consent screen, custom scopes or your own rate-limit quota.

prerequisites.text: A GitHub account, or admin access to the organization that should own the app.
A public homepage URL and the callback (redirect) URL of your integration. If you use Composio custom auth, copy the callback URL Composio shows you.

steps.title: Decide: OAuth app or GitHub App
steps.detail: Pick a GitHub App if you want fine-grained repository permissions and short-lived tokens; pick an OAuth app if you need enterprise-level resources or the simplest setup.

steps.title: Open Developer settings
steps.detail: Settings -> Developer settings -> OAuth Apps -> New OAuth App (shown as 'Register a new application' if you have never created one).

steps.title: Fill in name, homepage and callback URL
steps.detail: Use only public information. You can add up to 10 callback URLs. Enable Device Flow only if your agent runs where a browser redirect is not possible.

steps.title: Generate a client secret
steps.detail: Copy the client ID and client secret into your secrets store or your Composio custom auth config. Never commit them to code.

steps.title: Request only the scopes you need
steps.detail: Scopes are requested at authorization time, not approved by GitHub. Asking for fewer scopes makes users and org admins more likely to approve.

approval.summary: No GitHub review. Organizations can restrict third-party OAuth app access, so a user in such an organization may need an org owner to approve your app before it can see org resources.
triggers: Users in organizations with OAuth app access restrictions
approval.typical_wait: None from GitHub; depends on each organization's owner

blockers.problem: Users can sign in but see no organization repositories.
blockers.fix: The organization restricts OAuth apps. Ask the org owner to approve the app, or switch to a GitHub App installed on the org.

blockers.problem: Hitting rate limits as usage grows.
blockers.fix: OAuth app rate limits do not scale with installations; GitHub App installation tokens do.

blockers.problem: One account already owns 100 OAuth apps.
blockers.fix: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps; delete unused ones or use another owner.

agent_can: Choose between an OAuth app and a GitHub App from your use case
Prepare the name, homepage, callback URL and scope list
Check the finished setup against this guide
you_must: Sign in to GitHub and click through Developer settings
Generate and store the client secret
Ask organization owners for approval where needed
uncertain: Exact rate-limit numbers were not checked for this guide; see GitHub's rate-limit docs.

sources.title: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

guides.summary: Google is the hard case. Creating the OAuth client takes minutes, but most useful Gmail scopes are restricted. Before outside users can connect, Google requires app verification, and apps that access restricted data from a server need an annual security assessment by a Google-approved third party. Plan for weeks to months, not hours.

verdict.label: Hard
verdict.time_to_production: Up to 10 days for sensitive scopes; several months possible for restricted Gmail scopes
verdict.approval_required: Yes, for sensitive and restricted scopes

composio.note: Composio provides a managed OAuth app for Gmail. Bring your own only if you need your brand on the consent screen or custom scopes, and then you take on Google's verification yourself.

prerequisites.text: A Google Cloud project with the Gmail API enabled and the OAuth consent screen configured.
A public homepage and a privacy policy on a domain you own, verified in Google Search Console by a project Owner or Editor.
A justification for every sensitive or restricted scope, and a video showing how your app uses the data.

steps.title: Choose the narrowest scopes
steps.detail: Google requires the least access needed: an app that only reads mail must not ask for read-write-delete. Check each Gmail scope's category (non-sensitive, sensitive, restricted).

steps.title: Create the project and OAuth client
steps.detail: In Google Cloud Console: create a project, enable the Gmail API, configure the consent screen, then create an OAuth client ID with your redirect URI.

steps.title: Test with your own accounts first
steps.detail: You can build and test while verification is pending; users see an 'unverified app' screen until you pass.

steps.title: Verify your domain
steps.detail: Verify ownership of every authorized domain in Search Console with an account that is Owner or Editor on the project.

steps.title: Prepare the verification package
steps.detail: Homepage, privacy policy that matches how you use the data, scope justifications and a demo video.

steps.title: Submit in the Verification Center
steps.detail: Declare all scopes on the Data Access page and submit. Restricted scopes add a security assessment and re-verification every year.

approval.summary: Sensitive scopes need Google's OAuth verification; restricted scopes (most Gmail read/modify access) need a deeper review, and apps that reach restricted data through a third-party server need an annual security assessment by a Google-approved assessor. Some uses are exempt: personal use, development/testing/staging projects, internal-only apps in one Workspace organization, and domain-wide installation.
triggers: Showing your app name and logo needs brand verification even for non-sensitive scopes
approval.typical_wait: Sensitive: up to 10 days. Restricted: several months possible, plus yearly re-verification

blockers.fix: Expected until verification passes. Make sure the scopes in your code exactly match the consent screen configuration; a mismatch also triggers the warning.
Switch to the narrowest scope that supports your feature and explain the need in your justification.

blockers.problem: The security assessment cost and timeline.
blockers.fix: Budget for a paid third-party assessment and yearly renewal before you commit to restricted Gmail scopes, or use Composio's managed app.

agent_can: Map your feature to the narrowest Gmail scopes and their categories
Draft scope justifications and the privacy-policy sections Google checks
Write the demo-video script and a submission checklist
you_must: Create the Cloud project and OAuth client while signed in
Verify domain ownership in Search Console
Record the demo video, submit, and answer Google's reviewers
Arrange and pay for the security assessment if you use restricted scopes
uncertain: The user cap and refresh-token lifetime for apps in testing mode are commonly reported but were not confirmed in the pages read for this guide.
Security assessment price varies by assessor and was not checked.

guides.summary: Shopify depends on who your users are. Building for one merchant means custom distribution with no App Store review. Building for many merchants means public distribution, which requires App Store registration (a one-time fee) and Shopify's app review. The distribution choice cannot be changed later, and personal customer data needs a separate approval for public apps.

verdict.label: Medium (Hard if public)
verdict.time_to_first_connection: About 1 hour on a development store
verdict.time_to_production: Custom: same day. Public: after app review

composio.note: Shopify is not in Composio's managed OAuth list, so you must bring your own app.

prerequisites.text: A Shopify Partner or developer account and a development store for testing.
For public distribution: Shopify App Store registration, which has a one-time fee.

steps.title: Choose custom or public distribution
steps.detail: Custom for a specific merchant, public for many merchants. You cannot change it after selecting, so decide on the production app first.

steps.title: Create the app and set access scopes
steps.detail: Merchants approve your scopes at install time; a few scopes also need Shopify's own approval.

steps.title: Request protected customer data access if needed
steps.detail: Public apps need a separate approval for fields with customers' personal data.

steps.title: Test on a development store
steps.detail: Shopify expects you to find bugs on a development store before review.

steps.title: Public only: submit for app review
steps.detail: Fix every issue on the App Store review page, then submit. Status moves Draft -> Submitted -> Reviewed -> Published.

approval.summary: Custom apps need no App Store review. Public apps go through Shopify's app review, which can pause for core fixes before a reviewer is assigned; some scopes and protected customer data need separate approval.
approval.typical_wait: Not published on the pages read

blockers.fix: It cannot be changed; create a new app with the right method.
Shopify emails the required changes; fix them and click Submit fixes.

agent_can: Recommend custom vs public distribution from your user base
List the scopes and protected-data fields you need
Pre-check your app against the review requirements
you_must: Create the Partner account, app and development store
Pay the App Store registration fee if public
Submit for review and respond to the reviewer
uncertain: App review duration and the exact registration fee were not stated on the pages read.

guides.summary: Slack is medium difficulty. A new app installs only in its own workspace; to let other workspaces connect you must build an OAuth flow and turn on distribution, which needs no review. Slack Marketplace listing is optional but is reviewed, and some workspaces only allow Marketplace apps or need admin approval.

verdict.label: Medium
verdict.time_to_production: Same day for unlisted distribution; Marketplace listing takes Slack's posted review time and needs 10+ active workspaces first

composio.note: Composio provides a managed OAuth app for Slack. Your own app lets you control the bot name, scopes and Marketplace listing.

prerequisites.text: A Slack workspace where you can create and install apps.
HTTPS for every URL a distributed app uses, including the redirect URL.

steps.title: Create the app
steps.detail: Create the app in Slack's app dashboard; it is tied to one workspace at first.

steps.title: Add scopes and the redirect URL
steps.detail: Add bot and user scopes and your redirect URL (Composio's callback URL if you use Composio custom auth).

steps.title: Turn on distribution
steps.detail: Complete the distribution checklist so other workspaces can install via OAuth. Unlisted distribution needs no Slack review.

steps.title: Test on a second workspace
steps.detail: Install, onboard and uninstall on a workspace that is not your development workspace.

steps.title: Optional: submit to the Slack Marketplace
steps.detail: Only after the app runs on 10 or more active workspaces; Slack returns apps that are not ready.

approval.summary: Unlisted distribution has no review. Marketplace listing is reviewed against Slack's guidelines; review time varies with volume and is shown on your app's submission page, and Slack cannot speed it up.
triggers: Workspaces that only allow Marketplace apps or require admin approval
approval.typical_wait: Unlisted: none. Marketplace: see the estimate on your submission page

blockers.problem: A customer's workspace will not let users install your app.
blockers.fix: The workspace requires admin approval or Marketplace-only apps. Ask their admin to approve, keep scopes minimal, or get listed.

blockers.problem: You cannot submit to the Marketplace.
blockers.fix: Slack blocks submission until the app is installed on 10+ workspaces active in the last 28 days.

agent_can: Pick the bot and user scopes for your use case
Prepare the distribution checklist and Marketplace listing text
Check your redirect URLs use HTTPS
you_must: Create the app and install it while signed in
Turn on distribution and test on a second workspace
Get 10+ active workspaces before Marketplace submission
uncertain: Current Marketplace review time is shown only inside each app's submission page and was not observed for this guide.

guides.summary: Spotify looks easy but has a hard ceiling. New apps start in development mode, limited to 5 allowlisted users, and the owner needs Spotify Premium. Since 15 May 2025, Spotify accepts extended quota applications only from registered organizations with at least 250k monthly active users, so most new agent products can never leave development mode.

verdict.label: Blocked for most
verdict.time_to_production: Not possible for individuals or small products; for qualifying businesses, a partner application and app review
verdict.approval_required: Yes, to serve more than 5 users

composio.note: Spotify is not in Composio's managed OAuth list, so you must bring your own OAuth app.

prerequisites.text: A Spotify Premium account for the app owner (development-mode apps do not work otherwise).
To go beyond 5 users: a legally registered business with 250k+ monthly active users.

steps.title: Create an app in the Spotify Developer Dashboard
steps.detail: Add your redirect URI and copy the client ID and secret.

steps.title: Allowlist each test user
steps.detail: Add every user to the app's allowlist. Users who are not allowlisted can sometimes log in but get 403 errors on API calls.

steps.title: Check eligibility before planning a launch
steps.detail: Compare your organization against the extended-quota criteria before promising Spotify support to users.

steps.title: If eligible: partner application, then quota extension
steps.detail: After the Partner Application is approved, ask Spotify to move the app to extended quota mode; the app review team checks it against the Developer Policy.

approval.summary: Development mode needs no approval but caps you at 5 users. Extended quota requires an approved Partner Application (organizations only, 250k+ MAU) and an app review against Spotify's Developer Policy.

blockers.problem: Users get 403 errors after logging in.
blockers.fix: They are not on the allowlist, or the app already has its 5 development-mode users.

blockers.problem: You are an individual or early-stage startup and need more than 5 users.
blockers.fix: No supported path today. Tell users the integration is limited, or scope the agent to the owner's own account.

agent_can: Check your eligibility against the extended-quota criteria
Manage the allowlist checklist
Explain the 5-user limit to your users
you_must: Hold Spotify Premium and create the app while signed in
Add each user to the allowlist
Apply as an organization if you qualify
uncertain: Review time for Partner Applications is not published.
Older third-party articles cite a 25-user limit; the current docs say 5.

steps.detail: Write code to handle the authorization code callback, exchanging it via POST to the token endpoint using HTTP Basic Auth for client credentials.

steps.title: Handle rate limiting and errors
steps.detail: Incorporate logic to respect rate limit headers (HTTP 429 / 529), manage retry-after values, and gracefully catch user cancellations or missing redirect URIs.

blockers.problem: Missing redirect_uri in token exchange when multiple URIs are configured.
blockers.fix: Ensure the exact matching redirect_uri is supplied in the POST request to the token endpoint.
Read the Retry-After header and use exponential backoff with jitter.

prompts.plan:
A developer building an AI agent needs to register their own OAuth app with {app} and
get it approved for real users. List up to {n} URLs of {app}'s OFFICIAL developer documentation that
most likely cover: registering an OAuth app or integration, OAuth scopes or permissions, app review,
verification, publishing or approval, and limits before approval (test users, development mode,
rate limits). Use only the provider's own domains. Prefer specific documentation pages and include
the developer portal or docs home page as one entry. {retry_hint}
prompts.read:
Read these official documentation pages about {app}:
{urls}

Write concise research notes for a developer who must register their own OAuth app with {app} and
get it ready for real users. Cover: where and how to register (account type, redirect URI rules,
client secret), scopes and which ones trigger review, the review or approval process (who reviews,
requirements such as privacy policy, domain verification, video, business entity, minimum users,
fees, published wait times), limits before approval, common blockers with fixes, and which steps an
agent could prepare versus what needs a signed-in human.

Use only what the pages say. After each fact, put the URL of the page it came from. If the pages do
not answer something, write UNCONFIRMED instead of guessing. Today's date is {today}.

End with a line starting "MORE PAGES:" and up to 5 full URLs of documentation pages linked from these
pages that would answer what is still UNCONFIRMED (OAuth, scopes, app review, publishing).
prompts.structure:
Convert these research notes about {app} into the guide JSON.

Rules:
- Evidence: "docs" only when one of the official pages listed below supports the claim,
  "unverified" for anything else. Never use "tested" - nothing was tried by hand.
- "source" must be one of the URLs in the list below, or "" if none supports the item.
  Never invent a URL. "sources" lists the URLs you used, with short titles.
- difficulty: 1 = minutes, no review; 2 = minor checks; 3 = review only for some uses;
  4 = review or hard limits for most uses; 5 = weeks/months of review or effectively blocked.
  Judge it by what is required before OTHER people's accounts can connect. An optional
  marketplace, directory or app-store listing does not raise difficulty; mention it in approval.
  If the notes do not confirm a review, a limit or a block, do not assume one: use difficulty 3 with
  the label "Unclear" and list what is missing in "uncertain". Use 5 or "Blocked" only when a page says so.
- label: one or two words that match the difficulty, such as Easy, Medium, Hard or Blocked.
- Be specific about time and effort; if the notes give no number, say "not published" instead
  of guessing, and add it to "uncertain".
- Steps: 3-7 actionable steps in order. owner = "agent" when an agent can prepare or do it,
  "you" when a signed-in human must, "both" otherwise.
- Write for a developer who has never set this up before.
